text: Residual network, reverse edges, Dinic with current-arc.
labels: flow / capacity · max flow 50

A flow network (网络流) is a directed graph with a source s, a sink t and a capacity on every edge. A flow sends f(u, v) ≤ c(u, v) along each edge, and every node except s and t passes on exactly what it receives. Maximum flow (最大流): send as much as possible from s to t (P3376).

Greedy "push along any path" can get stuck. The fix is the residual network (残量网络): for each edge with flow f, there is room c − f forward and a reverse edge with room f, so later paths can undo earlier choices. A path from s to t in the residual network is an augmenting path; when none exists, the flow is maximum.
Algorithm Idea Time (worst case)
Ford– Fulkerson any augmenting path, by DFS O(m · maxflow), can be slow Edmonds– Karp shortest augmenting path, by BFS O(n m²)
Dinic BFS builds levels; DFS sends a blocking flow along level-increasing edges, many paths per round O(n² m); very fast in practice, O(m√n) on unit / bipartite graphs

Store each edge and its reverse at indices i and i ^ 1, so the partner is one XOR away. The current-arc pointer it[u] (当前弧优化) remembers where u stopped, so a saturated edge is never scanned again in the same round; without it Dinic can be far slower.
Use long long for capacities and the answer, reset it[] before every DFS phase, and make sure the reverse edge starts with capacity 0 (for an undirected edge, give both directions capacity c).
Max-flow min-cut; modelling choices as cuts.

An s–t cut splits the nodes into S (containing s) and T (containing t); its capacity is the total capacity of edges from S to T. Max-flow min-cut theorem (最大流最小割定理): the maximum flow equals the minimum cut capacity. After Dinic finishes, S = nodes still reachable from s in the residual network.

Min cut is a modelling tool: build a graph where "cutting an edge" means "paying a cost" or "giving up a choice". Every s–t path is a set of choices that cannot all be kept, so the cheapest way to break all of them is the min cut.

text: Grid selection (P2774): no two chosen cells may share an edge. Neighbouring cells have different colours in a chessboard pattern, so every conflict is a black–white pair. Each s → black → white → t path is a conflicting pair; the ∞ edge can never be cut, so the cut must drop one of the two cells.
Dropped cells = cut edges, so kept sum = total − min cut. The ∞ edge must be large but not overflow when added: LLONG_MAX / 4.
Hungarian algorithm; matching as flow; König.

A bipartite graph (二分图) has a left side and a right side, with edges only between them. A matching picks edges with no shared endpoint. Maximum matching (P3386): as flow, s → each left (1), left → right (1), each right → t (1); max flow = max matching. Dinic does this in O(m√n).

The Hungarian algorithm (匈牙利算法) is shorter: for each left node, try to find an augmenting path by DFS: take a free right node, or a right node whose partner can move elsewhere. O(nm), and only a dozen lines.
Left 1 takes right 1. Left 2 also wants right 1, so left 1 moves to right 2. Left 3 wants right 2, so left 1 would have to move again; but right 3 is free, so left 3 takes it. Three pairs.

König's theorem: in a bipartite graph, maximum matching = minimum vertex cover. Minimum path cover of a DAG = n − maximum matching (split each node into an "out" and an "in" copy). Pilots (P2756) and the hotel (P1402, two matchings chained through the guest) are matching models.
Cheapest augmenting paths with SPFA.

Minimum-cost maximum flow (最小费用最大流): every edge also has a cost per unit of flow. Among all maximum flows, find the cheapest (P3381). Successive shortest paths: repeatedly find the cheapest augmenting path in the residual network (reverse edges have cost −w), push as much as it allows, and repeat.

Reverse edges carry negative costs, so the shortest path needs SPFA / Bellman-Ford (第10章), or Dijkstra with potentials. Each augmentation keeps the current flow the cheapest one for its size, which is why the final maximum flow is the cheapest.

48 return 0;
Here the paths are taken cheapest first: 4 → 2 → 3 (cost 3, 20 units), 4 → 3 (cost 3, 20 units), then 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 (cost 16, the last 10 units): 60 + 60 + 160 = 280.

Cost-flow models: balancing loads around a ring (P4016), the napkin plan (P1251: day nodes, buy / fast wash / slow wash edges with costs), two disjoint routes with the most cities (P2770: split each city into in → out with capacity 1 and cost −1). Splitting a node into in / out with an edge between them is how a node capacity or node cost is expressed.

Flow problems are mostly about building the graph; the algorithm is a template. Draw the graph for the sample by hand before coding, and count nodes carefully when you split nodes or add a super source / sink.

Key points to memorise
1. Residual room: forward c − f, reverse f; augmenting path ⇒ more flow.
2. Edges in pairs i, i ^ 1; reverse edge starts at 0.
3. Dinic: BFS levels, DFS along level + 1 with current-arc; repeat while t is reachable.
4. Max flow = min cut; S side = reachable from s in the residual graph.
5. Cut models: ∞ edges forbid, cut edges pay; answer often total − min cut.
6. Max weight closure: s → positive, negative → t, item → prerequisite ∞.
7. Bipartite matching: Hungarian O(nm) or flow; König: matching = vertex cover.
8. Cost flow: SPFA cheapest path, reverse edge cost −w.
9. Node capacity or cost: split into in → out.
